title: Takeaways from ResearchED NYC
author: Lauren Brown
summary: Lauren Brown reports from ResearchED NYC, synthesising key takeaways from five sessions across the day. A recurring theme is that the science of learning -- specifically how memory, knowledge-building, and deliberate practice work -- is conspicuously absent from standard teacher training, a gap Zaretta Hammond frames as a moral failure. Deans for Impact presenters demonstrate that novice teachers consistently misidentify the more cognitively effective classroom activity. Nidhi Sachdeva argues that expert teaching requires both the science of learning and the craft developed through deliberate practice, and that the science component should come first, in initial training. Brown concludes with Sachdeva's caution that professional development too often prioritises exposure over practice, leaving teachers inspired but unchanged by Monday morning.
points: Zaretta Hammond opened by linking the science of learning directly to racial equity: 'When we don't get our students thinking, we are abandoning our #1 responsibility,' naming cognitive redlining -- over-scaffolding and over-simplifying -- as a justice issue.

Most novice teachers, before training in the science of learning, incorrectly identify the less cognitively effective classroom activity as superior; Deans for Impact's goal is to make learning science foundational in initial teacher education, not an add-on.

Nidhi Sachdeva's formulation -- 'We can't develop what we can't name' -- positions careful definitional work on what teaching actually involves as the prerequisite for deliberate practice and expert development.

Expert teaching sits at the intersection of science and craft: the science should be acquired first, in training; the craft begins there but deepens through experience and thoughtful professional development.

Professional development frequently prioritises exposure over practice; teachers leave conferences inspired but, facing Monday morning, return to their prior defaults -- the tools of the science of learning, applied to teachers' own practice, are the corrective.
quotes: Antiracism is not enough to disrupt what she referred to as 'cognitive redlining.' When we don't get our students thinking, we are abandoning our #1 responsibility: learning. Making school too easy, over-scaffolding, focusing on completion over understanding do our students no favors.

A key point about how human beings learn is everywhere at ResearchED, but I never saw it in my teacher training or any professional development. As Lynn Gaffney said at the final panel discussion of the day, 'I feel like I've been lied to.'
The most important sentence of her presentation was, 'We can't develop what we can't name.' So carefully defining the work we do is imperative.

Expert teaching, she went on, lies at the intersection of science and craft. The science should come, ideally, in teacher training, before they start actually teaching. The craft part begins then, too, but continues through experience and thoughtful professional development.

Professional development is clearly sorely needed to help teachers improve. She cautions, however, that we often prioritize exposure over practice. We leave conferences like ResearchED, feeling inspired. Great. But then with the reality of Monday morning, we often continue to do the same things we have always done.
The key is to use the tools of the science of learning -- deliberate practice -- to hone our craft. Not easy, to be sure. But unforgivable not to try.
